questions.prompt: Which observation proves a nonzero translation cannot be represented by a 2×2 linear matrix alone?
questions.answer: Every linear matrix sends (0,0) to (0,0), but a nonzero translation does not.
questions.explanation: Multiplying any 2×2 matrix by the zero vector gives zero. A nonzero translation sends the origin to its translation vector, contradicting that property.
questions.hint: Test the simplest input: the origin.
options: Every translation changes the area of a shape.
A 2×2 matrix can only rotate and never stretch.
Every linear matrix sends (0,0) to (0,0), but a nonzero translation does not.

questions.prompt: A new stretch A multiplies x by 4 and y by 2. Apply A to v = (1,3), then rotate 90 degrees counterclockwise. What is the final x coordinate?
questions.explanation: The stretched vector is (4,6). A counterclockwise quarter-turn gives (−6,4), so x is −6.
questions.hint: Respect the stated order and keep the intermediate vector visible.

questions.prompt: A linear map has matrix [[2,1],[0,3]]. By what positive factor does it scale area?
questions.explanation: Its determinant is 2·3 − 1·0 = 6. For planar area, use the absolute determinant, so the area scale is 6. The off-diagonal shear term does not change this value here.
questions.hint: Compute the 2×2 determinant ad − bc, then use its magnitude for ordinary area.

questions.prompt: U scales both coordinates by the same factor 3, and R is any rotation about the origin. Which statement is true?
questions.answer: RUv = URv for every vector v.
questions.explanation: U = 3I. Since rotations are linear, R(3v) = 3R(v), which is exactly equality of the two orders for every vector.
questions.hint: Uniform scaling multiplies the entire vector by one scalar; use linearity of rotation.
options: RUv = URv for every vector v.
The orders agree only when v is the zero vector.
No scaling can commute with a rotation.

projects.title: Compare averages without confusing a sample with the whole
projects.subtitle: Explore sample variation, fair selection and weighted comparisons.
projects.decision: Choose and interpret a sample-based estimate while explaining how selection and natural sample variation limit the conclusion.
projects.context: A tiny synthetic population contains six task times: A = 2, B = 4, C = 4, D = 6, E = 8 and F = 12 minutes. Its known population mean is 6 minutes. The lab enumerates subsets so you can see exactly how a sample mean changes; these are invented data for reasoning, not measured claims about a real workplace.

quantities.meaning: Number of units in the finite synthetic population
Number of distinct units selected without replacement
Signed error of the sample mean in this known-population demonstration

assumptions: The six labeled tasks are the entire synthetic population. The two tasks taking 4 minutes remain distinct units.
A sample contains n distinct units, with 1 ≤ n ≤ 6; sampling is without replacement.
The sample-index control enumerates possible subsets deterministically. It is not a random draw.
Only under simple random sampling of size n is each subset of n labeled units equally likely. The expectation statements explicitly use that design.

The real population mean is known here only to inspect sampling error. In a real estimation problem it is usually unknown. No confidence interval or empirical reliability claim is inferred from a single selected subset.

why.title: A mean balances a total across observations
why.text: The arithmetic mean divides the total measured time by the number of tasks, giving minutes per task. It is a center summary, not a claim that every task takes that long or that all samples must have that mean.

why.title: Different subsets can give different answers without arithmetic errors
why.text: The first three values have mean 10/3 minutes, while the last three have mean 26/3 minutes. Both calculations are correct. What they estimate, and whether they tend to favor particular values, depends on how those subsets were selected.

why.title: Random sampling concerns the selection procedure
why.text: Under simple random sampling, every allowed subset of the same size has equal probability. Picking the first few convenient cases or dragging a control to a favorable sample is not that procedure. A sample that happens to match the population mean does not prove its selection method was unbiased.

why.title: Variation of the data differs from variation of an estimate
why.text: Task times differ within the population. Sample means also differ across repeated selections. Larger simple random samples from this fixed population have less sampling variance, reaching zero when n = N; this does not guarantee that every particular larger sample is closer to μ.

why.title: Averaging group means requires their weights
why.text: If two groups have different sizes, their overall mean is not generally the average of their two means. Reconstruct each group total as count times mean, add the totals, and divide by the combined count. Changing group composition can even reverse an apparent comparison.

examples.title: Calculate an estimate and inspect its actual error
examples.prompt: Find the full population mean, then compare the first-three and last-three subset means.

steps.why: Include each labeled task exactly once, including both distinct tasks with time 4.
Divide the total by the number of units in the whole population.
This selected sample has three units, so its own total is divided by 3.
A different equally sized subset uses a different total.
Subtract the known population mean to quantify the signed errors. This comparison is possible because the complete synthetic population is visible.

examples.conclusion: Equal sample sizes do not ensure equal estimates. These two deliberately chosen subsets miss the population mean in opposite directions; neither deterministic choice is a random sample.

examples.title: Explain what unbiased means without promising a perfect draw
examples.prompt: If every three-unit subset is equally likely, why is the expected sample mean 6 even though individual sample means vary?

steps.why: Count ordered choices of three different units, then divide by the 3! orders representing the same subset.

steps.math: Each labeled unit belongs to (5·4)/(2·1) = 10 subsets
steps.why: After including one particular unit, choose its two partners from the other five.

steps.math: Sum of all 20 sample means = (10/3)·36 = 120 minutes
steps.why: Across all subsets each population value appears 10 times, and each subset mean divides its sum by 3.
Equal probabilities make the expectation the ordinary average over the 20 possible sample means.
steps.restriction: This step requires simple random sampling, with all 20 labeled subsets equally likely.

steps.why: The three smallest and three largest values supply the extremes, so one random sample can still be far from the expectation.

examples.conclusion: Unbiased means the selection procedure averages to the population mean across its possible draws. It does not mean every draw is accurate, representative in every respect or certain to include extreme values.

misconception.claim: A larger sample must give an estimate closer to the true mean on every individual attempt.
misconception.why: A larger simple random sample reduces sampling variance in this finite population, but particular samples can still fall in different places. Selection bias also is not automatically removed by collecting more cases the same biased way.
misconception.counterexample: The two-unit subset {B = 4, E = 8} has mean 6, exactly the population mean. The larger three-unit subset {A = 2, B = 4, E = 8} has mean 14/3, farther from 6.

prediction.prompt: Keep the synthetic population fixed and compare all simple random samples of size 3 with all samples of size 6. What changes?
options: At size 6 the individual task times all become 6.
At size 6 there is only the full population, so every sample mean is 6.
At size 6 the mean doubles because the sample is twice as large.
prediction.answer: At size 6 there is only the full population, so every sample mean is 6.
prediction.explanation: Sampling all six distinct units without replacement leaves only one possible subset. Its mean equals μ = 6, so sampling variability of the mean is zero. The six individual task times retain their original spread.

challenges.prompt: Use the subset control to inspect all 20 samples of size 3. Record their means, find the minimum and maximum, and count how many are within 1 minute of μ = 6, including the boundaries. Explain why that fraction is a sampling probability only under an equal-probability selection design.

Two synthetic teams handle different mixes of tasks. Team A: 2 morning tasks averaging 4 minutes and 6 evening tasks averaging 8. Team B: 6 morning tasks averaging 5 minutes and 2 evening tasks averaging 9. Compute each overall mean, then compare within morning and within evening. Explain why the aggregate ranking reverses and why it does not alone establish which team causes faster work.

Design a survey of task times across a full week. State the population, the selection procedure, how you would include different shifts, and what you would report besides one mean. Identify a source of bias that a large sample would not automatically fix, and explain what evidence would be needed for a reliable comparison.

rubric: Define the population, sample and quantity being estimated.
Use the correct denominator and retain duplicate-valued but distinct units.
Distinguish deterministic subset exploration from a random selection procedure.
Describe both variation and possible selection bias without guaranteeing accuracy from sample size.
Weight group means by their counts and avoid turning association into a causal claim.

transfer.prompt: A website compares the average completion time of two page designs. What must be checked before concluding that one design makes people faster?
transfer.connection: The weighted-mean issue transfers to mixtures of novice and experienced visitors. Comparable assignment, consistent outcome definitions, sampling variation and missing data matter. Random assignment helps support a causal comparison; random sampling addresses representation, which is a different question.

questions.prompt: Four synthetic task times are 3, 5, 7 and 9 minutes. What is their arithmetic mean, in minutes?
questions.explanation: The total is 24 minutes across four tasks. Dividing 24 by 4 gives a mean of 6 minutes.
questions.hint: Add all four times, then divide by the number of tasks rather than by the number of different values.

questions.prompt: A selected sample contains times 2, 4 and 12 minutes. What is its mean, in minutes?
questions.explanation: The sample total is 18 minutes and the sample size is 3, so its mean is 18/3 = 6 minutes. A correct mean alone does not identify the selection procedure.
questions.hint: Use the sample total and the sample count, including every selected unit.

questions.prompt: Two task-time datasets have the same mean. What can you conclude from that fact alone?
questions.answer: Their centers by the arithmetic-mean measure match, but their spreads may differ.
questions.explanation: A mean summarizes total divided by count. It does not determine the individual values, range, shape or variability, so those may be different.
questions.hint: Compare the pairs {5,5} and {0,10}: their means agree but their values are spread differently.
options: Every corresponding task time must be equal.
Their centers by the arithmetic-mean measure match, but their spreads may differ.
Both datasets must have zero variability.

questions.prompt: From six labeled tasks, how many different unordered samples of three distinct tasks are possible without replacement?
questions.explanation: There are 6·5·4 ordered triples. Each unordered subset is counted in 3·2·1 orders, so the number of subsets is 120/6 = 20. Identical measured values do not make distinct labeled tasks the same unit.
questions.hint: Count ordered selections first, then remove the multiple orders of each three-unit subset.

questions.prompt: In a known synthetic population the true mean is 7 minutes. One selected sample has mean 9 minutes. What is its signed estimation error x̄ − μ, in minutes?
questions.explanation: Signed error is sample estimate minus population value: 9 − 7 = +2 minutes. The estimate is 2 minutes too high.
questions.hint: Follow the subtraction order specified in x̄ − μ; do not take an absolute value unless asked.

questions.prompt: Two different labeled tasks both take 4 minutes. In simple random sampling of labeled tasks, how should they be treated?
questions.answer: As two distinct eligible units, even though their measured values match.
questions.explanation: Sampling units are the tasks, not the set of unique numerical values. Removing one repeated value changes the population and the probabilities.
questions.hint: Separate the identity of an observation from its measured value.
options: As one unit because repeated measurements never count twice.
As units that cannot appear in the same sample.
As two distinct eligible units, even though their measured values match.

questions.prompt: One group has 2 tasks with mean 4 minutes. A second group has 6 tasks with mean 8 minutes. What is the combined mean, in minutes?
questions.explanation: Reconstruct totals: 2·4 = 8 and 6·8 = 48 minutes. The combined total is 56 across 8 tasks, giving 7 minutes. Averaging 4 and 8 equally would ignore the unequal group sizes.
questions.hint: Multiply each group mean by its count, add those totals and divide by the combined count.

questions.prompt: A survey of service speed includes only customers served during the quietest shift. What should be addressed before generalizing to all shifts?
questions.answer: The selection procedure may omit systematically slower or busier conditions.
questions.explanation: A sample from one selected shift need not represent the target population across all shifts. Collecting more observations only from that shift does not automatically remove the selection problem.
questions.hint: Ask which members of the intended population had a chance to be included.
options: The selection procedure may omit systematically slower or busier conditions.
No issue remains once the sample contains 100 observations.
The arithmetic mean is invalid for any service-time data.

questions.prompt: Page Design A has a lower observed mean time than B, but A was used mainly by experts and B mainly by beginners. Which conclusion is justified?
questions.answer: The aggregate difference alone does not establish that design caused the time difference.
questions.explanation: Visitor experience is mixed differently across the designs and may affect completion time. A fair causal comparison needs comparable assignment and other relevant checks, not only two means.
questions.hint: Look for a difference between the groups besides the design being studied.
options: Design A has been proved faster for every user.
The aggregate difference alone does not establish that design caused the time difference.
The lower mean guarantees less variation in times.

questions.prompt: A new synthetic sample has task times 1, 3, 5 and 11 minutes. What is its mean, in minutes?
questions.explanation: The total is 20 minutes and there are four observations, so the mean is 20/4 = 5 minutes. The large value 11 contributes to the total just like each other observation.
questions.hint: Compute the full sum before dividing by the sample size.

questions.prompt: A new report combines 3 tasks averaging 10 minutes with 5 tasks averaging 6 minutes. What is the combined mean, in minutes?
questions.explanation: The group totals are 30 and 30 minutes. Together there are 60 minutes across 8 tasks, yielding 60/8 = 7.5 minutes. Equal totals do not mean equal group sizes.
questions.hint: Recover the totals from count times mean, then divide the overall total by the overall count.

questions.prompt: For a fixed finite population with nonzero variation, simple random sampling without replacement uses n units. What happens as n increases toward the full population size?
questions.answer: The sampling variance of the mean decreases, but each particular draw is not guaranteed to be closer to the true mean.
questions.explanation: The random-selection procedure becomes less variable in aggregate and has zero sampling variance at a census. That property of the distribution of estimates is not a guarantee about any one realized sample.
questions.hint: Distinguish average behavior across all possible samples from a promise about a particular selected subset.
options: Every individual task time moves closer to the population mean.
Every larger selected sample is guaranteed to give a more accurate mean than every smaller sample.
The sampling variance of the mean decreases, but each particular draw is not guaranteed to be closer to the true mean.
